newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Hyder eyed for H1 div rise, savings.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Hyder eyed for H1 div rise, savings.

text.p: British multi-utility Hyder, formed when Welsh Water took over regional electricity company (Rec) South Wales Electricity, may pay a strong interim dividend and report a rise in half year profits on November 22.
It could also give further details on anticipated cost savings from the 872 million stg agreed bid, analysts said.
"Strong dividend growth and more information on cost savings, that is what we will be looking at," said one sector analyst who asked not to be named.
Hyder is expected to turn in half year pretax profits between 96 and 109 million stg, up from the 80.6 million stg it achieved as Welsh Water a year ago.
It is expected to lift its dividend to between 14.35 and 14.7 pence per share, up from 12.6 pence previously.

Hyder said in June that cumulative cost savings from the merger should total 275 million stg by the year 2000, with eight million stg coming through in the first year, while benefits could cut operating costs by 46 million stg in 2000.
"It would be interesting to get a better picture of how the group is combining, say with another indication of cost savings," the sector analyst said.

United Utilities, which was the first multi-utility to be created when North West Water took over local Rec Norweb last year, has indicated real dividend growth may be 11 percent and predicted cost savings of 105 million stg in 1997/98.
Analysts will also be watching the performance of Hyder's non-core businesses, such as construction consultancy.

The group's 40 percent stake in CableTel South Wales, acquired in the merger, was bought in October by International CableTel Incorporated, which used $78 million of non-voting convertible preferred stock to fund the deal.

Hyder holds a 40 percent stake in UK Highways, a consortium which won a contract in October to improve, run and maintain 122 kilometres of the M40 motorway between London and Warwick in central England.
Other members of the group are Tarmac and John Laing which each hold 20 percent, France's Caisse des Depots et Consignations which has 16 percent and Transroute International with four percent.
Hyder has said its regulated water and electricity businesses will remain core but that it looks to its infrastructure expertise for future extra dividend growth.

Analysts are hoping Hyder will not overstretch itself outside its core operations."I hope there are no big surprises on diversification. More, greater, benefits will come from integration of Welsh Water and Swalec," the sector analyst said.
